title: The Game of Sixty-Four Squares
summary: Kāṇha plays a board game with compassion as its pihāṛi: he breaks up and kills the pawns, his fine elephant churns up the five people, and by intelligence he brings the king to parinirvāṇa, conquering the forces of existence through the true guru's teaching; at the end he counts the sixty-four squares and takes them. Munidatta introduces the song as the same meaning set out again through the contemplation of a game of dice (cp.12.m1). He reads the pieces as stages of yoga: the pawns as the hundred and sixty natures, the elephant as the lord of yogis' suchness-mind, the king as the mind of ignorance, made one on which parinirvāṇa is superimposed, and the squares as the sixty-four compartments of the wheel of emanation, where Kāṇha takes his own mind, clear light by nature (cp.12.m3 to cp.12.m6).

flags.note: The heading line itself reads only '[rāga] bhairavī'. The poet's name is supplied from the attribution kṛṣṇapādānām ('of Kṛṣṇapāda'), which the edition prints before the song and which the emendation removed from line 1a; the Tibetan heading also names the poet (nag po zhabs). Drop '· Kāṇha' if the heading should carry only what the line has.

lines.gloss: compassion · pihāṛi (sense uncertain: board? seat?) · (I) play · naa (naya 'way, strategy'? or nava 'new, nine'?) · strength, forces
lines.en: [Compassion]{karuna} the [pihāṛi]{pihari}, I play with strategy and strength;

flags.note: pihāṛi is of uncertain sense and is kept in source form, as the glossary directs. It may name the board or the seat the game is played on (compare Bengali piṛi, 'low wooden seat'). Munidatta explains it as the seven faults, stains of samādhi, which are split and removed (cp.12.m2); the Tibetan translation has rgyal mtshan, 'victory banner', in the line and rgyal, 'victory', in its comment.

naa bala: Munidatta divides it naya and bala and glosses them 'the secret of the way of mantra' and 'the strength of the fourth joy' (cp.12.m2). I follow his division and render naya by a plain sense that suits a game, 'strategy' (it also means 'way, conduct, policy'), and bala as 'strength'. naa could equally be nava, 'new' or 'nine' ('with new forces', 'with nine pieces'), and bala also means 'army, forces', as in bhababala in 1b. The Tibetan line has rgyan po rtse bar byed, 'plays at a wager (a game of chance)', and its comment treats rgyan po as the word being glossed, as if naa bala named the game or the stake.

karuṇā pihāṛi: two nouns side by side, taken here in apposition ('compassion as the pihāṛi'). Munidatta comments on them as separate words (cp.12.m2); the Tibetan joins them with a genitive, snying rje'i rgyal mtshan, 'the banner of compassion'. khelahum̐ is first person, like dehum̐ and lehum̐ in couplet 5; the Tibetan (rtse bar byed) and Munidatta ('playing ... conquered by us') agree.

lines.gloss: true-guru · by-understanding, by-teaching (bodha, instrumental) · conquered · forces-of-existence
lines.en: Through the true [guru]{guru}'s teaching I have conquered the [forces of existence]{bhavabala}.

flags.note: bohem̐ is the instrumental of boha (Sanskrit bodha), literally 'understanding, awakening'. I render 'teaching' because Munidatta has 'from the instruction of the vajra guru' (vajragurorupadeśāt, cp.12.m2) and the Tibetan has bla ma'i gsung gis, 'by the guru's word'. A more literal line would be 'By the true guru's awakening'.
jitela has no expressed subject; 'I' follows the first person of 1a and Munidatta's 'conquered by us, Kṛṣṇācārya' (cp.12.m2).

lines.gloss: cut off, broken (phīṭ-, past) · two, pair · mādesire (sense uncertain; Tibetan 'to the side') · king
lines.en: The two are cut off in the [king]{thakura}'s quarter;

flags.note: mādesire is not glossed by Munidatta and its division is uncertain. The Tibetan translation renders the line phyogs su Du a bskul na rgyal po la, 'when the Du a is pressed to the side, toward the king', which takes -desire as deśa, 'region, quarter' (phyogs), and makes ṭhākura the goal ('toward the king'). I follow that sense with 'in the king's quarter', but it leaves mā- unexplained. Other divisions: mā desi re, 'do not give, O (king)', with de- 'give' as in dāha dehum̐, 'I make a move', in 5a; or māde sire, with sire 'on the head'. Please decide, or keep the word in source form.

phīṭau duā: Munidatta says phīṭa means 'cut off' (niḥkṛntita) and takes duā as the pair (dvaya) of appearances (cp.12.m3). The Tibetan does not translate duā but spells it Du a, as if it were a technical word, perhaps a throw of the dice ('deuce'); its verb bskul, 'press, urge', is explained in its comment as 'cutting off'. I render 'the two are cut off'.

lines.gloss: taāri (uncertain; read as upakāri 'helper' by Munidatta and the Tibetan) · instruction (upadeśa) · Kāṇha · near (nikaṭa) · city-of-the-Jina (jinapura)
lines.en: By the helper's [instruction]{upadesa}, [Kāṇha]{p-kanha} is near the [city of the Jina]{jinapura}.

flags.note: taāri has no clear sense. Munidatta's gloss 'by the helper's instruction' (upakārikopadeśena, cp.12.m3) and the Tibetan phan thabs, 'helpful means' (its comment has 'the means of one who helps', phan par byed pa po'i thabs), both read upakāri, which would be uaāri in Old Bengali; Shastri's taāri may be a misreading of it. I have adopted 'helper'.

jinaura: the Tibetan line has rgyal ba'i pho brang, 'the Victor's palace', which supports jinapura, 'city of the Jina', the glossary's reading. Munidatta instead has 'the presence of the best of Jinas' (jinavara[sya] sannidhānam, cp.12.m3), as if reading jinavara. The Tibetan comment has rgyal po'i pho brang, 'the king's palace'.

lines.en: First I broke up the [pawns]{baria} and killed them;

flags.note: The Tibetan translation reads dang por mi reng bton na gsod par 'gyur, 'first, when the mi reng is brought out, it is killed': it has 'brought out' (bton) for toṛiā, 'having broken', as if reading toliā (as in 3b), and makes the killing passive and conditional. mi reng, its word for baṛiā, is of unclear sense.
No subject is expressed; I supply 'I', as in 1a and 5a. The form marāṛiiu is unusual (perhaps a causative of mār-, 'kill'); the sense 'killed' is supported by the Tibetan gsod.

lines.gloss: by-the-fine-elephant (gaja-vara, instrumental) · having-lifted · five-people · churned, stirred up
lines.en: The fine [elephant]{elephant} lifted and churned up the [five people]{pancajana}.

flags.note: gaabarem̐ is instrumental (Munidatta repeats it as gaavareṇa, 'by the fine elephant', cp.12.m4), so the elephant is the agent or instrument; I make it the subject. The Tibetan instead has glang chen bton nas, 'having brought out the elephant', with the elephant as the object of toliā. toliā, 'having lifted', has no expressed object; in a game it may mean picking pieces up off the board.

gholiu is from ghol-, 'churn, stir': here 'churned up', perhaps 'threw into confusion'. The Tibetan has skye bo lnga dang rtses, 'played with the five people'. Munidatta's paraphrase has the ornament of the five struck down and the five made 'without pride' (nirmada) (cp.12.m4). Who the five people are in the game is not said.

lines.gloss: by-intelligence · the-king (object, -ka) · brought-to-parinirvāṇa (parinirvṛta; or parinivṛtta, 'wholly stopped')

flags.note: parinibittā is rendered with the glossary's parinirvāṇa, as Munidatta (parinirvāṇa, cp.12.m5) and the Tibetan (yongs su mya ngan 'das) take it. It might instead reflect parinivṛtta, 'brought wholly to a stop', which would suit a king stopped in the game, as in checkmate.

-ka marks ṭhākura as the object, so an unexpressed agent acts on the king; I supply 'I'. The Tibetan makes the king the subject: blo yis rgyal po yongs su mya ngan 'das, 'by intelligence the king passed into parinirvāṇa'.

lines.gloss: helpless (avaśa; or avaśya, 'certainly') · having-made · forces-of-existence · conquered
lines.en: Making him helpless, I conquered the [forces of existence]{bhavabala}.

flags.note: The Tibetan translation has nges par byas pas srid pa'i dpung las rgyal, 'by making certain, (I) won over the army of existence', as if reading avaśya, 'necessarily, certainly', for abaśa. Munidatta's paraphrase, suvyagrasamagraṃ kṛtvā (cp.12.m5), is of unclear sense and reflects neither plainly. I follow the Bengali: avaśa, 'powerless, helpless'.
abaśa kariā has no expressed object. I supply 'him', the king of 4a (helpless like a king that cannot move); it could equally be the forces of existence ('making them helpless').

lines.translit: bhaṇai kāhnu āhme bhali dāha dehum̐
lines.gloss: says · Kāṇha · we (= I) · good, well · move · (I) give

flags.note: dāha is rendered 'move', the glossary's reading (compare Bengali dān, Hindi dā̃v, a turn or throw in a game; the idiom is 'give a move'). Munidatta renders it dāya, 'gift', explained as the intention of an exceptional offering (cp.12.m6); the Tibetan has bde mchog bzang, 'supreme bliss is excellent', with no verb for dehum̐.
āhme is formally 'we', used of the speaker, as often in the songs; rendered 'I'. bhali may be an adjective ('a good move') or an adverb ('I move well').

lines.en: I count the sixty-four [squares]{kotha} and take them.

flags.note: lehum̐, 'I take', has no expressed object; I supply 'them', the squares. The Tibetan (re mig drug cu rtsa bzhi rtsis nas len, 'having counted the sixty-four squares, takes') leaves it open too; Munidatta supplies 'my own mind' (cp.12.m6).

notes.text: Rāga: a melodic mode of Indian music; each song's heading names the one to which it is sung. Bhairavī is the rāga of this song; the word is also a name of a goddess.

The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) heads the song rnga bo che zhes bya ba'i glu'i dbyangs nag po zhabs kyi'o, 'the melody called Great Drum; of Nag po zhabs (Kāṇha)'. rnga bo che, 'great drum', may reflect a reading of the rāga name as bherī, 'kettledrum'. The poet's name in the English heading comes from the attribution kṛṣṇapādānām, 'of Kṛṣṇapāda', which the edition prints before the first line and which the emendation removed from 1a.

The song is a game. Its pieces, a king (ṭhākura), pawns (baṛiā), an elephant (gaavara) and 'five people', and its board of sixty-four squares (koṭhā) point to a board game like chess, whose early Indian form, caturaṅga, was played on a board of eight by eight squares. Munidatta instead introduces the song as the same meaning set out again 'through the contemplation of a game of dice' (dyūtakrīḍādhyānena), presumably the meaning of the preceding song, also Kāṇha's (cp.12.m1); some board games of this kind were played with dice. The draft translates the moves as moves and does not name the game.

Where Munidatta's introduction has 'through the contemplation (dhyāna) of a game of dice', the Tibetan translation of it has rgyan po 'gyed pa dgongs pa'i skad kyis, 'in the intentional language of gambling', as if it read or understood a reference to twilight language in place of 'contemplation' (cp.12.m1).

pihāṛi (kept in source form): a word of uncertain sense, joined to compassion at the opening of the game; it may name the board, or a seat (compare Bengali piṛi, 'low wooden seat'). The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has rgyal mtshan, 'victory banner', in the line and rgyal, 'victory', in its comment, as if its translators read or understood a different word.

naa bala. Munidatta takes naa as naya, 'way, method', glossed 'the secret of the way of mantra', and bala as 'strength', glossed 'the strength of the fourth joy, that very bodhicitta' (cp.12.m2). Old Bengali naa could also come from nava, 'new' or 'nine', and bala also means 'army, troops', the sense it seems to have in bhababala. The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) renders the pair rgyan po, 'wager, game of chance' (rgyan po rtse bar byed, 'plays at a wager'), and its comment glosses rgyan po as the secret of the way of mantra and the strength of the fourth joy. The draft has 'strategy and strength'.

Munidatta reads couplet 1 as yogic union (cp.12.m2). Compassion is the mind in the form of the self-blessing mind (svādhiṣṭhānacitta); pihāṛi is the seven faults connected with its support (āśraya), the stains of samādhi, which are split and removed; naya is the secret of the way of mantra; bala is the strength of the fourth joy, bodhicitta itself. Playing by the vajra guru's instruction, in the union of vajra and lotus, the two as one, with unbroken joy, 'we, Kṛṣṇācārya' have easily (akleśavaśena) conquered the forces of existence, which he explains as the force of the appearance of sense objects. The Tibetan comment adds that victory over the seven faults is called non-apprehension (dmigs pa med), and for 'easily' has nyon mongs pa'i dbang gis, 'through the power of the afflictions', as if without the negative.

bhababala joins bhava, 'existence', and bala, 'strength' and also 'army, troops'. In a game with a king, an elephant and pawns, the forces of existence are apparently the opposing side. The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has srid pa'i stobs, 'power of existence', here and srid pa'i dpung, 'army of existence', at 4b.

Munidatta explains the forces of existence as the force of the appearance of sense objects (viṣayābhāsabala) (cp.12.m2), and at 4b as the force of the host of things (bhāvagrāma), the sense objects beginning with form (cp.12.m5); the Tibetan renders bhāvagrāma as dngos po'i grong, 'the town of things'.

Munidatta names couplet 2 as the refrain (dhruvapada) (cp.12.m3) and counts couplets 3, 4 and 5 as his second, third and fourth verses (cp.12.m4, cp.12.m5, cp.12.m6). In the edition the cue ধ্রু, 'sing the refrain', stands after couplet 1 as well as after the refrain and the later couplets; it is not translated.

Munidatta reads the first line of the refrain through vajra recitation: by its process the pair of appearances (ābhāsadvaya) is first cut off; the king is the mind of ignorance (avidyācitta), named together with 'the helper's instruction' in a gloss that has no verb (cp.12.m3). The Tibetan construes the gloss as 'by the means of one who benefits the mind of ignorance'.

On the second line of the refrain Munidatta says that at the end of passion, when the joy of cessation arises, through the instruction on imperishable bodhicitta and by unbroken joy, Kṛṣṇācārya came of himself into the presence of the best of Jinas and was united with it (the Sanskrit is loosely built) (cp.12.m3). He supports this with a verse of Daṛatīpāda: at the end of passion, at the moment of entering cessation, when the moon stands in its own nature and the course of the wind is stopped, the bliss that arises then and nowhere else is directly the supreme state, and one who experiences it is accomplished through Mahāmudrā.

The Tibetan translation of Munidatta's comment (cp.12.m3) differs in two places: it has byang chub kyi sems mi 'gyur ba, 'unchanging bodhicitta', for bodhicittākṣara, confirming akṣara as 'imperishable' rather than 'syllable'; and where the Sanskrit has Kṛṣṇācārya coming into the presence of the best of Jinas, it has nag po spyod pa rgyal po'i pho brang rang nyid kyis nye bar 'joms par gyur pa, apparently 'Kṛṣṇācārya himself came to conquer near the king's palace'. It names the author of the verse u Da'i zhabs.
baṛiā are apparently the pawns of a board game (compare modern Bengali boṛe, 'pawn'): pieces broken up and killed first, as pawns are early in a game of chess.

Munidatta introduces couplet 3 as his second verse, on the progression of excellence in practice, and calls vaṛikā (the song's baṛiā) twilight language (sandhyābhāṣā) for the hundred and sixty natures (prakṛti), which are first made without intrinsic nature through the process of vajra recitation (cp.12.m4).

gaavara is gaja, 'elephant', with vara, 'excellent', perhaps simply the elephant piece of the game; toliā is from tol-, 'lift, raise'; pāñcajanā, 'five people', may be pieces of the game, though in Bengali 'five people' can also mean people at large. The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has glang chen bton nas skye bo lnga dang rtses, 'having brought out the elephant, he played with the five people'.

Munidatta reads the fine elephant as the lord of yogis' suchness-mind, lord of elephants (tathatācittagajendra). With it the ornament of the five sense objects, which consist of the five aggregates, namely I-making, mine-making and the rest, is struck down; the objects are made 'without pride' (nirmada, a word also used of an elephant out of rut); and realization follows (sākṣātkṛtam; the Tibetan says selflessness is made manifest) (cp.12.m4). His paraphrase puts the five sense objects where the song has the five people, without an explicit gloss.

parinirvāṇa (kept in source form): complete or final nirvāṇa, classically the passing of a buddha at death. Here the king of the game is brought to it; see the flag on the alternative reading parinivṛtta, 'brought wholly to a stop'.

Munidatta introduces couplet 4 as his third verse. 'By intelligence' means by understanding in accord with the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitānubuddhi); the king is the mind on which affliction had been superimposed, now made one on which parinirvāṇa is superimposed; and so the forces of existence, the host of things, the objects beginning with form, were conquered 'by us' (cp.12.m5). He quotes Nāgārjuna: by the very mind by which fools go into bondage in saṃsāra, yogins go to the state of the sugatas. The Tibetan says intelligence is to touch the perfection of wisdom.

The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) reads the line kAh+Nas smras pa bdag ni bde mchog bzang, 'Kāṇha says: for me supreme bliss is excellent' (or 'I am excellent supreme bliss'), with bde mchog, 'supreme bliss', where the Bengali has dāha and no verb for dehum̐. Its comment explains bde mchog as 'by the intention of thinking of things as they truly are', where Munidatta has 'the intention of an exceptional offering' (cp.12.m6).

Munidatta introduces the last couplet as Kāṇha's praise of his own seat of yoga (yogāspada). He renders dāha as dāya, 'gift', meaning the intention of an exceptional offering, and has Kṛṣṇācārya say: having made it steady in the wheel of emanation (nirmāṇacakra) with its sixty-four compartments, I take my own mind, clear light by nature (cp.12.m6). The sixty-four squares of the board thus become the sixty-four compartments of the wheel of emanation; the Tibetan has re mig and re'u mig, 'squares', for both.
Sixty-four squares: the board of eight by eight squares on which chess-like games were played. Kāṇha counts them and takes them, apparently claiming the whole board at the end of the game.

termsOmitted.reason: Tibetan-side hit only: rgyan in the Tibetan line is part of rgyan po, 'wager, game of chance', which renders naa bala; it is not rgyan, 'ornament', and the Bengali has no ornament.
Tibetan-side hit only: thabs in phan thabs, 'helpful means', is the Tibetan's rendering of uesa (upadeśa), which the English renders with the glossary's 'instruction' (upadesa).
Tibetan-side hit only: rtsa in drug cu rtsa bzhi is the linking word of the numeral 'sixty-four', not rtsa, 'channel'.

questions: 2a (refrain): mādesire is unresolved. I followed the Tibetan (phyogs su, 'to the side') and wrote 'in the king's quarter', which leaves mā- unexplained. Would you prefer the division mā desi re, 'do not give (a move), O king', or keeping mādesi in source form with a note?

1a: naa bala is rendered 'strategy and strength' after Munidatta's division into naya and bala. nava, 'new' or 'nine' ('with new forces', 'with nine pieces'), is also possible, and the Tibetan takes the pair as the wager or game itself (rgyan po). Which do you want?
1a: pihāṛi stays in source form as the glossary directs. If you accept 'board' (after Bengali piṛi), the line could read 'Compassion the board, ...'; should the glossary entry change?
2b: I adopted upakāri, 'helper', from Munidatta and the Tibetan over Shastri's taāri, which has no clear sense. Confirm, or keep taāri as an unexplained word?
4a: parinirvāṇa follows the glossary; parinivṛtta, 'brought wholly to a stop', would fit the game (a king that is stopped). Keep the glossary rendering here?
Heading: I added '· Kāṇha' from the attribution kṛṣṇapādānām. Should it read Kāṇha, Kāṇhapāda or Kṛṣṇapāda (the example heading in the brief has Lūyīpāda)?

Person: the first person of khelahum̐, āhme ... dehum̐ and lehum̐ is rendered 'I' throughout, and 'I' is supplied in 1b, 3a, 4a and 4b, where no subject is expressed. Acceptable, or should those lines be passive ('the pawns were broken up and killed')?

Game: the draft does not say whether the game is played with dice (Munidatta's dyūta, the Tibetan's rgyan po) or is chess-like (king, elephant, pawns, sixty-four squares). Should the title or a note commit?
4b: abaśa is read as 'helpless', with 'him' (the king) supplied as object; the Tibetan reads 'certainly' (avaśya). Keep?
